source.title: Disentangling MLP Neuron Weights in Vocabulary Space
source.authors: Asaf Avrahamy; Yoav Gur-Arieh; Mor Geva

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates language-model neuron behavior using a new weight-space decomposition and channel-ablation approach, rather than reproducing the original vision-neuron method.
record.gate_note: The paper tests whether decomposed channels correspond to distinct neuron behaviors, but it does not estimate the share of all neurons that are polysemantic. Its SAE and other decomposition-baseline scores are comparisons of methods, not direct measurements of neuron polysemanticity, and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It takes neuron polysemanticity as a premise and introduces ROTATE to break neuron weights into vocabulary channels. All quantitative results score ROTATE's own output: faithfulness and completeness versus SAE and random baselines, channel-ablation selectivity, and description win rates. It never measures what share of neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how this varies by layer, or what causes it. High faithfulness or completeness shows that the decomposition works, not how polysemantic the neurons are. The reader's T2/tests reading and its V2 'supports' label are not warranted.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that ROTATE recovers faithful, causally separable vocabulary channels from MLP neuron weights, without data. These channels beat SAE baselines on faithfulness and completeness and yield better neuron descriptions. They present the channels as a scalable, though not exhaustive, unit of analysis.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weight-space rotations to maximize vocabulary-projection kurtosis, then channel ablations and channel-description evaluations; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model and layer: the reported faithfulness and completeness scores differ across the four tested model-layer combinations. The authors also note stronger gains in middle-to-late layers and identify vocabulary alignment as a limitation.

fits_no_version.finding: One Gemma-2-2B-it neuron (L18 N9005) decomposes into gate channels for temporal markers, polarity/negation, GUI programming tokens and place-name subwords. Each passes a faithfulness t-test. Shown qualitatively, not as a prevalence estimate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual LM MLP neurons can be decomposed into several separately faithful, semantically distinct weight-space components (anecdotal evidence of polysemantic neurons).

fits_no_version.finding: 97.1% of ROTATE channel top tokens fall outside the raw neuron projection's top-200 tokens (20 Gemma gate neurons).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The raw vocabulary projection of a neuron hides most of its component concepts, so judging a neuron's semanticity from its raw projection understates its mixture.

fits_no_version.finding: Vocabulary kurtosis of neuron weights is higher for known concept neurons than for random neurons. In OLMo-2 it rises during training and concentrates in middle and late layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vocabulary-projection kurtosis is a proxy for neuron monosemanticity, and it varies by layer and training stage.

record.problems: The main evaluations cover 100 randomly sampled neurons per selected layer and only two selected layers per model in the main setup. The faithfulness test uses synthetic examples generated from channel descriptions, and completeness and description evaluations rely on LLM judges. The paper notes that vocabulary-orthogonal functions are outside ROTATE's scope.
record.rows_left_out: Not included: SAE-based and other decomposition-baseline scores in Table 1 and §E.1, as they compare methods rather than directly measuring neuron polysemanticity; description-generation head-to-head wins in Figure 4 and §6, as they evaluate descriptions rather than the neuron behavior itself; other optimization and hyperparameter ablations in §C.6–C.7, which concern ROTATE procedure choices rather than the claim.

untested.parts: The share of MLP neurons that respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how it varies by layer, are not measured. Only method performance on 100 random neurons per layer is reported.
Superposition as a cause is not tested.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure is not tested.
No comparison across activation functions, architectures or regularization of polysemantic share.
There is no test of whether canonical polysemantic neurons are actually monosemantic generalizations.

There is no test of how polysemantic classification depends on activation range or scoring. Description win rates differ by activation-rank range, but this compares description methods, not polysemanticity labels.

record.verdict_notes: The study relies on polysemanticity as motivation (citing Gurnee et al., Bricken et al.) but does not quantify it. All rows are the method's own performance or validation scores, so they are relinked to 'none'. The reader's V2 'supports' label is dropped.

versions.untested_parts: The prevalence of polysemantic neurons across language models; whether a large share of neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts; broad layer and model coverage.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
Whether polysemanticity arises from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
Effects of activation functions, architecture, or regularization on the share of polysemantic neurons, and performance costs of reducing that share.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons, including the cited InceptionV1 neuron, detect one shared feature or related offshoots rather than unrelated mixtures.
Whether the classification of neurons as polysemantic changes with activation range or explanation-scoring method.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B-it
rows.operation_detail: Projected the top channel out of the gate weight and measured the ablated-to-original neuron activation ratio.
rows.note: The text says ablating the activated channel drives its activation ratio toward 0; exact figure values are not stated.
rows.check: The input-side ablation ratio validates that the channels are separable components. It says nothing about whether the channels' concepts are unrelated, or how common such neurons are.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B-it
rows.operation_detail: Described distinct input-side and output-side vocabulary channels for a sampled neuron.
rows.measure: Qualitative account of neuron activations and promoted/suppressed concepts
rows.value: The neuron is described as activating positively on technical negation/polarity text and negatively on temporal-deferral constructions; its output channels are described as carrying distinct polarity, code-syntax, and temporal concepts.
rows.note: A single illustrative neuron, not an estimate of how common such neurons are.
rows.check: A single illustrative neuron, apparently picked for display. It shows one mixed-concept neuron but cannot bear on V2's 'large share' or layer claims. Better recorded under fits_no_version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Evaluated channels in the tested layers of Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
reader_labels.reason: Channel descriptions correspond to activating inputs above chance, channel ablations selectively reduce neuron activations or decoded channel tokens, and the illustrated neuron has distinct described functions (R1–R25).
